A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Causal Diagnosticity research framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions and relocation of material.

before.justification: v1 reports original diagnosticity measurements across four tasks, with knowledge-editing, explanation-type and model-size experiments in the main text and appendix.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmarking results and additional corruption-sensitivity and task-complexity analyses, including results in Appendices D and E.

M1.justification: The framework's central scoring procedure changes from counting strict wins to assigning wins, ties and losses scores of 1, 0.5 and 0, respectively. Continuous CoT metrics also switch from absolute to signed prediction-score changes. v2 introduces syntax-aware Early Answering and alternative filler replacement procedures, while retaining the knowledge-editing approach to constructing explanation pairs.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same four tasks: COUNTERFACT-based fact checking, city/capital analogies, object counting and StrategyQA-based multi-hop reasoning. The added corruption and complexity analyses reuse this coverage; they do not introduce new datasets, domains or task requirements.

E2.justification: Counterfactual Edits is removed from the main, MEMIT and model-generated-explanation comparisons: v1 Tables 1, 3 and 4 correspond to v2 Tables 1, 4 and 5. The four retained CoT-corruption comparators undergo substantive scoring revisions from absolute to signed differences, and modified Early Answering and Filler Tokens variants are explicitly compared.

E3.justification: v2 changes the diagnosticity evaluation metric through neutral tie handling and adds Copeland aggregation for overall rankings. Appendix E adds accuracy evaluation under direct and CoT prediction, including hop-count breakdowns. The reported paraphrasing prompt also changes from antonym substitution in v1 Figure 15 to paraphrasing in v2 Figure 16; this establishes a documentation-level protocol revision without establishing whether earlier experiments used the displayed prompt.

E4.justification: New analyses test filler symbol and repetition choices, syntax-aware truncation, and corruption-induced prediction-score changes (Section 5.2 and Appendix D.2). Appendix E.2 adds task-accuracy and reasoning-depth analyses, while Table 7 supplies worked corruption examples. Existing editing-method, explanation-type and scaling analyses are retained, with scaling moved to Appendix A.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly adds 95% bootstrap confidence intervals to edit-reliability and scaling plots, among others. It replaces the previous McNemar/binomial testing approach with Wilcoxon signed-rank and one-sample t-tests, and adds significance reporting to further comparisons. Neither PDF establishes an increase in repeated runs or supplies seed counts.

E6.justification: Many main and appendix results change. In Table 1, Gemma's FactCheck Filler Tokens score changes from 0.280 to 0.893, and Qwen's FactCheck Simulatability score from 0.013 to 0.501. These are revised measurements under changed scoring definitions, not directly comparable performance gains. v2 also adds filler-choice results and task-accuracy findings.

T1.justification: v2 replaces the strict-comparison diagnosticity estimator with a piecewise mathematical definition awarding half credit to ties (Equations 3–6), explicitly addressing the 0.5 random baseline. Together with the signed continuous-score definitions, this changes the quantities being measured rather than merely their notation. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace the emphasis on metrics frequently failing the random baseline with task/model-dependent performance and Filler Tokens performing best overall. The continuous-metric advantage is narrowed from all comparisons in v1 Section 5.5 to most comparisons in v2 Section 5.6, with sensitivity to noise and model choice foregrounded.

C2.justification: v2 adds important applicability restrictions: metrics must accept externally supplied explanations and provide per-instance scores, explaining why Counterfactual Edits is unsuitable. It develops v1's OOD-sensitivity hypothesis through interpretations of corruption choices and small score changes, adds task-complexity interpretations, and redirects future work toward locating unfaithful reasoning steps.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the promise of future code/data release with a code-repository link, supplies explicit truncation heuristics and worked scoring examples, and corrects the displayed paraphrasing prompt. Most existing model choices and generation prompts remain. The explicit city-dataset source link present in v1 is removed; repository contents cannot be established from the PDFs.

R1.justification: v2 adds Lyu et al.'s faithfulness survey and Tutek et al.'s work on unlearning reasoning steps. The latter informs the expanded discussion of internal interventions and sentence-level assessment. The main positioning relative to diagnosticity, knowledge editing and existing faithfulness metrics remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, technical background, results narrative and conclusion receive extensive rewriting. The experimental narrative gains a dedicated sensitivity section, the model-size discussion moves into Appendix A, and the appendices are reorganized into more explicit implementation, sensitivity and task-complexity subsections.

P2.justification: Figure 2 changes from a two-by-two arrangement to four horizontal task panels. v2 adds sensitivity and accuracy plots, a multipage worked-example table and a filler-variant table; existing tables gain overall-ranking columns and plots gain uncertainty displays. The binary/continuous comparison moves into the main text, while scaling displays move to the appendix.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses central evaluation weaknesses: tied scores no longer count as failures, and the incompatible Counterfactual Edits comparison is removed with an explicit rationale. Added uncertainty reporting and targeted sensitivity analyses substantially strengthen the evidence and qualify the conclusions. Reporting problems remain: Table 7's paraphrasing score conflicts with its formula, and Appendix A's Filler Tokens scaling description conflicts with Figure 7 and Table 3. These problems limit confidence in individual statements but do not outweigh the improvements to the comparative framework.
